title: The al-Ruwāfa bilingual (Petrantoni 47) — a Nabataean Aramaic and Greek temple dedication by the natio of the Thamud for Marcus Aurelius Antoninus and Lucius Aurelius Verus, naming Claudius Modestus and Quintus Antistius Adventus
language_note:
A BILINGUAL, and the tier has no other. The chapter sets the monument as five lettered sections: A, C and E are Greek; B and D are Nabataean Aramaic, printed in Latin-script transliteration and not in Nabataean characters. Each section is followed by its own English translation, and the sections interleave rather than running as two parallel columns — C opens at line 5b, where B ended at 5a.

THE LANGUAGE CODES ARE A CHOICE AND THIS RECORD DECLARES IT RATHER THAN INHERITING ONE. `arc` is written for the Nabataean Aramaic, following arabia-02-palmyrene-tariff, which carries `arc` for another Aramaic dialect in another bilingual. arabia-03-jsnab17 IS NABATAEAN AND CARRIES `xna` PLUS `arb` — Ancient North Arabian and Arabic — which is a different answer to the same question, made before this record existed and not amended here. The two records now disagree about how to code one language and the disagreement is on the record rather than smoothed, because a code changed to match would move that record's digest for a reason nothing in its own commit explains. Whichever is right, this is a defect of the corpus's vocabulary and not of either record's reading.

The Greek is printed unaccented throughout the edited text and fully polytonic in the footnotes — Ἀντιστίου, Σεβαστῶν, σισόη — so the absence of accents in the sections below is the edition's epigraphic convention and not a stripped diacritic. That control is worth stating: it is what rules out the failure FINDING 48 measured.
date: 164/166–169 CE. The dedication is dated by the honorands' titles and the two Greek sections DO NOT CARRY THE SAME SET: section A gives (Α)ρμενια(κ)ων alone, section C adds [Μηδι]κων (Πα)ρθικ(ω)ν με(γ)[ι](σ)των. THIS RECORD DOES NOT DERIVE A DATE FROM THAT DIFFERENCE. The range is the one the edition and the hunt carry; the divergence in titulature is recorded as an observation about the text, and narrowing either section from it would be this project supplying a reading of its own — FINDING 55.

original_text_note:
Verbatim from the per-chapter PDF, PASTED BY THE CURATOR from Petrantoni entry 47, pp. 121–128, on 2026-09-05. This session did not open the chapter: the capture is blind on the model's side, which is the whole of the reason the three findings below were available to be found.

EDITORIAL ACTS, DECLARED. The section letters A) B) C) D) E) are supplied by this record as labels; the chapter labels the sections but does not print them inline in the running text this way. Blank lines separate the sections. The numerals 1) 2) 3) 4) 5a) 5b) 6) 7) 8) 9) 10) are the EDITION'S OWN line numbers and are kept, because they are how the two languages are keyed to each other across the monument — B ends at 5a and C begins at 5b, and an excerpt that dropped them would lose the interleaving. The PDF's soft line wraps are closed up; no word is split across one. NOTHING ELSE IS ALTERED — every bracket, parenthesis, underdot, caron, angle bracket and the stray space before the closing bracket in `60 letters ]` stands as printed.

FINDING 1 — THE LACUNA NOTATION IS ENGLISH PROSE INSIDE THE EDITED TEXT, AND IT IS SET IN ITALIC THAT PLAIN TEXT CANNOT CARRY. `[lacuna of approximately 14 letters]` is literally what the edition prints — confirmed against a screenshot of the page, not inferred — where most editions print a symbol such as `[- - - ca. 14 - - -]`. In the page image the descriptions are ITALIC and the restored text is ROMAN, which is how a reader tells the editor's description from the text; and in line 2 `[θνος lacuna of approximately 60 letters ]` puts BOTH INSIDE ONE PAIR OF BRACKETS, with `θνος` restored text and the rest description. Stripped to plain text the two are indistinguishable. A reader of this excerpt cannot tell which characters the monument carried, and this record says so rather than inventing a marker to separate them. ONE FURTHER OBSERVATION FROM THE SAME IMAGE, RECORDED AND NOT ACTED ON: that one description in line 2 appears to be set roman where the others are italic, which if it is right is an inconsistency in the edition and not in this capture.

FINDING 2 — THE DISPUTED SEQUENCE IN SECTION E IS ENCODED THREE DIFFERENT WAYS IN ONE CHAPTER AND NO TWO AGREE. The opening of inscription E appears in the edited text, in its English translation, and in the commentary on p. 128, and the three differ character by character in whether each glyph is Greek or Latin:
  p. 128, Milik's reading      Ϲ·grk  I·lat  Ϲ·grk  Θ·grk  A·lat  Ι·grk  Ο·grk  Ι·grk
  section E, edited text       E·lat  C·lat  Y·lat  C·lat  Θ·grk  Α·grk  Ι·grk  T·lat  Ο·grk  Y·lat
  section E, translation       E·lat  Ϲ·grk  Y·lat  Ϲ·grk  Θ·grk  A·lat  I·lat  T·lat  O·lat  Y·lat
The ordinary Greek of the same PDF is clean and fully polytonic, so this is not a general encoding failure: it is localised to precisely the letters that are epigraphically uncertain, which the edition sets with per-letter alternatives — `(E)/(Ϲ)` and `(Ι)/(T)` mean 'read this letter as either'. THE ENCODING IS A DEFECT AND THE ALTERNATIVES ARE A CONTESTED READING, AND THE TWO ARE NOT THE SAME THING — the distinction this hunt already drew when it refused AbSWS 79 for being a text its own editors flag as wrong. THE EXCERPT IS NOT NORMALISED. Choosing lunate sigma over Latin C is choosing Milik's reading, and a reading this project supplied itself is worth nothing (FINDING 55). It also matters mechanically: this corpus is byte-addressed by archived citation spans, and Ϲ U+03F9 and C U+0043 are different tokens to the embedder, so the sequence in this excerpt and the sequence in this record's reference_translation are NOT the same string and a gold case must not assume they are.

FINDING 3 — WHAT THE CAPTURE DID NOT GO WRONG ON, MEASURED RATHER THAN ASSUMED. Every `[` matches a `]` across all five sections; parentheses balance once the line numbers are discounted; `š ḥ ṣ ṭ ḏ ṯ ḡ ō ā` are all present as precomposed NFC characters; and the ayin and alef are U+2018 and U+2019, not the U+0027 that FINDING 48 measured a fetch producing. This is the first capture in this tranche to be checked mechanically before it was written, and it passed.

THREE READINGS IN THIS INSCRIPTION ARE DISPUTED BETWEEN NAMED EDITORS, AND THE EDITION PRINTS BOTH SIDES OF EACH. They are given verbatim below, from the pages the curator read. Footnote reference numerals, which paste inline as bare digits, are removed; nothing else is altered, and the edition's own slips — `Antonius` for Antoninus, a missing `in` before `order to recreate`, `ha cons(e)crated` in the translation of C — stand as printed.

1. THE LAST WORD OF SECTION B, w(r)mṣhm, AND THE EDITION'S OWN TRANSLATION FOLLOWS MACDONALD AGAINST MILIK. From p. 126: "At the end of the line we read the verb rmṣ probably meaning ‘to pacify’, used only in Nabataean with this meaning; according to Milik, who proposed this interpretation, it is a loanword coming from Arabic ramaṣa bayna ‘to make peace between’, ‘réconcilier des ennemis, mettre la paix entre eux’. By contrast, Macdonald suggests that this translation is philologically impossible because here ramaṣa is not followed by bayna, but by the plural pronoun -hm whose translation ‘made peace between them’ appears to be unacceptable; so, according to Macdonald the form is a maṣdār, i.e. ramṣ and the sentence wa-ramṣ-hum would mean ‘and at their request’." THE READING IS UNCERTAIN AND THE DISPUTE IS UNRESOLVED IN THE EDITION. Section B's translation above ends 'and at their request', which is Macdonald's reading and not Milik's — so this record carries a source text established on one reading and a published translation that follows the other, with the disagreement printed between them.

2. THE OPENING SEQUENCE OF SECTION E, WHICH THREE SCHOLARS READ THREE WAYS. From p. 128: "In the inscription E the initial sequence, which Milik originally read ϹIϹΘAΙΟΙ (on the copy of Philby), turns out to be problematic in its interpretation." And from the note to that sentence: "According to Van den Branden it could be a graphic representation of the Arab custom to cut the hair and to shave the temples, in fact, considering O rather than Θ, he reconstructs the word σισόη translating it as ‘manière de couper les cheveux en rond’, also ‘roll of hair’ (LSJ, 1601); but this suggestion proves to be contrived (Macdonald et al. 2015, 54 and fn. 138). For further considerations, see Graf 1978, 10". THE READING IS UNCERTAIN: the edition prints the sequence with per-letter alternatives, states that Milik's reading is problematic, gives Van den Branden's alternative in full, and rejects it on a third scholar's authority without substituting a reading of its own.

3. WHAT STOOD IN SECTION B AFTER THE EMPERORS' NAMES. From p. 126: "In the Nabataean text, after the references to Antonius and Verus, Milik originally reconstructs ’rmny’ ‘Armenians’, but Macdonald points out that there is not enough space between m and final ’ order to recreate the ethnonym." THE RESTORATION IS UNCERTAIN AND THE EDITION LEAVES IT SO: the excerpt above prints that stretch as `dy ’[---]’`, an unfilled gap, rather than adopting either scholar's text.
reference_translation_note: The English is Petrantoni's own, printed section by section after each edited text in the same chapter, so the published-translation test is met on the page itself and not by citation-of-record. It is a translation of a bilingual and the two languages are translated separately: A, C and E render the Greek, B and D the Nabataean. THE TWO DO NOT SAY THE SAME THING and the record does not treat them as parallel witnesses — B names the ’pkl, the priest Ša‘aḏaṯ, where the Greek sections do not, and C carries the Roman officials' titles where B carries only Adventus's name.

notes:
F5 Part 3, and the first of the tranche's two Arabia verbatim_with_provenance slots.

WHAT IT SAYS ABOUT ROME. A temple on the north-west Arabian frontier, built by the natio of the Thamud and dedicated for the eternal duration of the power of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus and Lucius Aurelius Verus, styled Armeniaci and — in section C — Medici and Parthici Maximi, the titles of the eastern war. The Roman administration is present in it by name and by office: Claudius Modestus with the title of propraetor, and Adventus, whom the edition's footnote identifies with the legatus Quintus Antistius Adventus. The Nabataean sections name what the Greek does not — the ’pkl, the priest Ša‘aḏaṯ son of Muḡīḏō of the tribe Roḇaṯō, and the god ’Ilahā to whom the building was made. It is a provincial community writing itself into imperial victory in its own language and in the empire's, on one monument, and the record carries both because it is a bilingual and not a translation.

WHY A BILINGUAL AND NOT A THIRD GREEK RECORD, WHICH IS THE OBJECTION THIS RECORD ANSWERS RATHER THAN WAITS FOR. Three of the five sections are Greek, and the corpus already carries one Greek text serving three regions — FINDING 62. This is not that. The Nabataean sections are the region's own language, the speakers are the Thamud, and source_language_provenance classifies this record on findspot, which is in the region. The tier has no other bilingual.

GLOSS-CAPABLE, contested_reading, AND STRONGER THAN ANY DECLARATION F3 OR F4 MADE. Three disputes, all between named identifiable editors — Milik against Macdonald twice, and Van den Branden against Macdonald once — all about how to READ the text rather than about which modern country an ancient name answers to, and all printed in the reachable edition. That is the discount ruling 62 had to take on eastasia-05-liangshu-qin-lun going the other way. THE MECHANICAL REQUIREMENT IS MET WHERE F3 LOST A DECLARATION: all three sit inside reference_translation, which the loader chunks, and none is in notes, which it does not.

TWO CORRECTIONS THE BLIND PASTE MADE TO THE HUNT, AND THEY ARE THE REASON THE CAPTURE RULE EXISTS. F5_CANDIDATES.md and F5_PART3_START.md both quote, as verbatim from p. 126, the sentence "Macdonald does not agree with this reading and, conversely, he points out that there are two ṭ" — AND THE CURATOR DID NOT FIND IT ON THAT PAGE. It remains unlocated in this chapter as of this record's date, and it is not used here. That is the second locating-fetch page reference this block has had corrected by a paste, after record 36's 24a/24b.

AND THE HUNT'S SECOND QUOTE WAS A TRUNCATION THAT CUT AWAY THE HALF THAT MATTERS. It carried "Macdonald suggests that this translation is philologically impossible because here ramaṣa is not followed by bayna" and stopped at the comma. The sentence continues, and what follows is MACDONALD'S OWN ALTERNATIVE READING — the maṣdār ramṣ, wa-ramṣ-hum, 'and at their request' — which is the reading Petrantoni's own translation of section B then adopts. A gloss built on the truncated quote would have said only that Milik is wrong; the page supports one that says what the text is read as instead, and shows the edition choosing it. THE HUNT'S VERSION WOULD HAVE PRODUCED A WEAKER RECORD THAN THE SOURCE SUPPORTS, and no amount of re-fetching would have shown that, because the fetch is where the truncation happened.

THE BOUNDARY, STATED. Petrantoni's chapter is the only edition read for this record. Milik's editio princeps, Macdonald et al. 2015 and Graf 1978 are all cited in the chapter and NONE of them was consulted: every quotation of Milik, Macdonald and Van den Branden above is Petrantoni reporting them. The dispute is therefore attested at one remove, in a peer-reviewed edition that names its sources — which is what makes it a published alternative rather than one this project supplied — but a reader who wants the arguments themselves must go to those three, and this record does not stand behind Petrantoni's characterisation of them.

THE PLACE THAT COULD NOT BE RESOLVED IS RECORDED AS A REFUSAL AND NOT AS AN ABSENCE — see findspot_places.

findspot_places.name: Al-Ruwāfa
findspot_places.note: NO PLEIADES PLACE FOR AL-RUWĀFA EXISTS IN THE PINNED SNAPSHOT AND ONE HAS NOT BEEN GUESSED. The 2026-08-10 names dump — data/pleiades-names-20260810.csv.gz, the dated snapshot this corpus resolves against — was searched directly for ruwafa, rawwafa and ruwāfa and returns nothing. THE SEARCH WAS RUN BY READING THE DUMP AND NOT THROUGH `--find`, because the session that wrote this record had no shell on the host; the dump is the same file `--find` reads, and re-running it through the tool would be worth doing. TWO NEARBY IDS WERE FOUND AND BOTH ARE REFUSED. Pleiades 814662 Tabūk resolves precisely, and Tabūk is a distance and a bearing this record uses to say where the site is — it is not the findspot, and placing the findspot on it would put a pin 75 km from the temple. Pleiades 814740 Thamudaei resolves as a rough polygon and is the ETHNONYM'S TERRITORY, not the site; it is used in subject_places, where the natio is what the text is about, and it must not be reused here to make the findspot look located. GEONAMES WAS NOT SEARCHED: it needs the SA country file downloaded and passed to `--geonames-find` on the host, which this session could not run, and PLACES.md is explicit that a GeoNames placement is a modern administrative place whose note must say what its coordinate denotes. That check is owed, and until it is made the honest ground is regional and the map is sparser for it.

subject_places.name: the natio of the Thamud (Θαμουδηνων εθνος, tmwdw)
subject_places.note: The people the whole monument is organized around: they found the temple in A, make it in B, complete and consecrate it in C, and build it in E. Pleiades 814740 Thamudaei, confirmed present in the pinned 2026-08-10 dump with a real polygon extent — 36.0–37.0 E, 27.0–28.0 N, roughly located, Roman period — so this is the `regional` form that draws an extent rather than a pin, which is what a people is. Ground `regional` and not `stated`: the text names the people, and a people's territory is not a specific place, so PLACES.md's requirement that `stated` name a point does not hold here.

subject_places.name: the tribe Roḇaṯō / Ροβαθου
subject_places.note: Named in section D as the priest Ša‘aḏaṯ's tribe and again in section E as the tribe that built the sanctuary — φυλης Ροβαθου. Placed because PLACES.md places every named place and this corpus already places a people (Thamudaei) as one; `mentioned` because nothing moves through it in this text. NO GAZETTEER ENTRY WAS SOUGHT AND NONE IS CLAIMED: the pinned dump holds no Robathos under any spelling tried, and a subdivision of the Thamud has no territory this record can point at that is not simply the Thamud's own.
